grammar.explanation: Turn a verb or adjective into a noun with ~기, attach the particle ~도, then finish with 하다. This adds a sense of 'also' to a whole action or description, and often implies the thing happens only some of the time ('sometimes does').

examples.ko: 저는 가끔 혼자 영화를 보기도 해요.
examples.en: I sometimes watch movies alone, too.
Sometimes tears come out when you cut onions.
That person also teaches chemistry.
I sometimes boil milk in the morning.

grammar.explanation: Link two ~기도 clauses: the first ends in ~기도 하고 and the second in ~기도 하다, conjugated for tense and politeness at the end. It stresses that both actions or both descriptions are true, like 'not only A but also B'. The two parts can be verbs or adjectives, even ones with opposite meanings.

examples.ko: 저는 주말에 책을 읽기도 하고 친구를 만나기도 해요.
examples.en: On weekends I read books and also meet friends.

examples.ko: 그 영화는 슬프기도 하고 재미있기도 했어요.
examples.en: That movie was both sad and fun.

examples.ko: 저는 대학교에서 철학을 공부하기도 하고 화학을 공부하기도 했어요.
examples.en: At university I studied both philosophy and chemistry.

examples.ko: 이 일은 쉽기도 하고 어렵기도 해요.
examples.en: This work is easy in some ways and hard in others.

grammar.explanation: To report what someone said, put the quoted verb in the plain (written) form and add ~고, then a verb like 하다 or 말하다. Present tense uses ~는다고 after a final consonant and ~ㄴ다고 after a vowel; past tense is ~았/었다고, and future is ~(으)ㄹ 거라고 or ~겠다고.

examples.en: My friend said he is going to Korea tomorrow.
My younger sibling said they finished all their homework.

examples.ko: 그 소설가가 새 책을 쓸 거라고 했어요.
examples.en: The novelist said she will write a new book.
The kids said they are planting trees.

grammar.explanation: Adjectives in the present tense take no extra syllable in the plain form, so you add ~다고 straight to the stem. Past tense still uses ~았/었다고. The reporting verb (하다, 말하다) carries the final tense and politeness.

examples.en: Minsu said he is very tired today.
The teacher said this problem is difficult.
My friend said that room is tiny.

grammar.explanation: When the quoted sentence ends in 이다, attach ~이라고 after a noun ending in a consonant and ~라고 after a vowel. The negative 아니다 becomes 아니라고. The same form is used to say what someone or something is called, as in introducing your name.

examples.en: That man said he is a doctor.
My friend said this is her bag.
That person said he is not a student.
My name is Kim Minsu.

grammar.point: Other verbs used with quotes (생각하다, 믿다, 약속하다, 부르다)
grammar.explanation: A quoted clause can come before verbs other than 말하다 when the content is a thought or statement. Common ones are 생각하다 (think), 믿다 (believe), 약속하다 (promise) and 부르다 (call something a name). Promises usually use a future quote such as ~겠다고 or ~ㄹ 거라고.

examples.en: I think this movie is fun.

examples.ko: 저는 우리 팀이 이길 거라고 믿어요.
examples.en: I believe our team will win.
I promised to pay back the debt by tomorrow.
Koreans call this gimbap.

grammar.explanation: Adding ~(이)라고 to 뭐 asks what someone said, with or without 했어요 after it. You can also repeat part of what someone said in quoted form with a rising tone (often with ~요) to check that you heard it correctly.

examples.en: What did the teacher say?
What did you say?
You said there's a test tomorrow?

grammar.point: Quoted clause before a noun: ~ㄴ/는다는 것/사실/소문
grammar.explanation: A plain-form clause plus ~는 can describe a noun, as a shortened form of ~다고 하는. It shows the content is something that was said or reported. It is especially common with nouns like 것, 사실 (fact) and 소문 (rumor).

examples.ko: 그 사람이 회사를 그만둔다는 소문을 들었어요.
examples.en: I heard a rumor that he is quitting the company.
I didn't know that my friend has a lot of debt.
I found out yesterday that my sister got married.

grammar.explanation: To report a 'let's...' suggestion, attach ~자 to the verb stem, then add ~고 and a reporting verb. It works the same no matter whether the stem ends in a vowel or a consonant.

examples.en: My friend suggested we watch a movie together.

examples.ko: 남자 친구가 주말에 바다에 가자고 했어요.
examples.en: My boyfriend suggested we go to the sea this weekend.
My younger sibling suggested we eat pizza for dinner.

grammar.explanation: When reporting a question, attach ~느냐고 or the more common, casual ~냐고 to a verb stem, usually followed by 묻다 or 물어보다. Past tense is ~았/었냐고. 있다 and 없다 follow the verb pattern.

examples.en: Mom asked me if I had eaten.
My friend asked me where I was going.
The doctor asked me if I smoke.

grammar.explanation: For adjectives, the formal pattern adds ~으냐고 after a consonant and ~냐고 after a vowel. In everyday speech many people just use ~냐고 for all adjectives.

examples.en: My friend asked me if I'm busy these days.
That person asked if the room is big.
Mom asked if the food was tasty.

grammar.explanation: When the quoted question ends in 이다, attach ~이냐고 after a consonant and ~냐고 after a vowel. Question words like 뭐 and 누구 often come right before it.

examples.en: That person asked me if I was a student.
My friend asked what this was.
The teacher asked who that man was.

grammar.explanation: To quote someone's exact words, put them in quotation marks and add ~라고 (or 하고), followed by 하다 or 말하다. The original words stay as they were said, with no change to plain form.

examples.en: The child said, "I'm hungry."
The man said, "Hello."
Mom said, "Come quickly."

grammar.explanation: To report an order or instruction, attach ~으라고 to a stem ending in a consonant or ~라고 to a stem ending in a vowel. Then add a reporting verb such as 하다 or 말하다. The person who received the order is usually marked with ~에게 or ~한테.

examples.en: The teacher told the students to read the book.
Mom told me to go to bed early.

examples.ko: 의사가 저에게 물을 많이 마시라고 했어요.
examples.en: The doctor told me to drink a lot of water.
The manager told me to attend the meeting.

grammar.explanation: To report 'don't do...', attach ~지 to the verb stem, then 말라고 (from 말다) and a reporting verb. It is the quoted version of ~지 마(세요).

examples.ko: 엄마가 저에게 늦게 오지 말라고 했어요.
examples.en: Mom told me not to come home late.

examples.ko: 선생님이 수업 시간에 떠들지 말라고 했어요.
examples.en: The teacher told us not to chat during class.

examples.ko: 의사가 저에게 술을 마시지 말라고 했어요.
examples.en: The doctor told me not to drink alcohol.

grammar.point: Quoted requests for oneself: ~(아/어) 달라고 하다
grammar.explanation: When the original speaker asked for something to be given to them, 주다 is replaced by 달다, giving 달라고. The same happens with ~아/어 주다 when they asked for something to be done for them (~아/어 달라고). This is true no matter who later reports the request.

examples.en: My younger sibling asked me to give them water.

examples.ko: 친구가 저에게 돈을 빌려 달라고 했어요.
examples.en: My friend asked me to lend him money.

examples.ko: 아이가 엄마에게 책을 읽어 달라고 했어요.
examples.en: The child asked mom to read him a book.
The customer asked us to close the window.

grammar.point: Giving to someone else: 주라고 하다
grammar.explanation: If the original speaker told someone to give something to a third person rather than to themselves, use the regular command quote 주라고. Choosing between 달라고 and 주라고 depends on who receives the item or the benefit.

examples.ko: 엄마가 저에게 동생한테 과자를 주라고 했어요.
examples.en: Mom told me to give my younger sibling some snacks.

examples.ko: 선생님이 저에게 이 책을 민수에게 주라고 했어요.
examples.en: The teacher told me to give this book to Minsu.

examples.ko: 친구가 저에게 그 편지를 여자 친구에게 주라고 했어요.
examples.en: My friend told me to give that letter to his girlfriend.

grammar.explanation: 부탁 means a favor or request and can be used as a noun. 부탁하다 means to ask a favor. It often follows a quoted request like ~아/어 달라고.

examples.en: I have a favor to ask.
I asked my friend to help me move.

examples.ko: 제 부탁을 들어 줄 수 있어요?
examples.en: Can you do me a favor?

lessons.title: Lesson 56: To make, to let: ~게 하다, ~게: so that

grammar.point: To make / let someone do: ~게 하다
grammar.explanation: Attach ~게 하다 to a verb or adjective stem to show that the subject causes someone to do an action or be in a state. Korean does not separate 'make' (force) from 'let' (allow), so context decides the English. The person affected is usually marked with ~을/를 or ~에게, or with ~이/가 when the clause has its own object.

examples.en: Mom made me go to bed early.
The teacher let the students go home.
That news surprised me.

examples.ko: 아빠가 동생이 게임을 못 하게 했어요.
examples.en: Dad didn't let my younger sibling play games.

grammar.point: So that / in a way that: ~게 + verb
grammar.explanation: ~게 can be followed by a verb other than 하다 to say what was done so that something happens. The clause with ~게 gives the purpose or result, and the main verb gives the action that brings it about. It is often used with ~ㄹ 수 있게 or ~지 않게.

examples.ko: 아이들이 잘 볼 수 있게 글씨를 크게 써 주세요.
examples.en: Please write big so the kids can see well.

examples.ko: 다른 사람들이 들을 수 있게 크게 말해 주세요.
examples.en: Please speak loudly so others can hear.
Leave early so you are not late.
I closed the window so the rain wouldn't come in.

grammar.explanation: For many 하다 verbs, swap 하다 for 시키다 to show that the subject makes or gets someone else to do the action. 공부하다 means to study yourself, while 공부시키다 means to make someone study. It does the same job as ~하게 하다.

examples.en: Mom makes my younger sibling study every day.
I got my two friends to make up.
That news disappointed my parents.

examples.ko: 친구가 저에게 좋은 사람을 소개시켜 줬어요.
examples.en: My friend introduced me to a nice person.

grammar.point: 시키다 as a verb: to order
grammar.explanation: On its own, 시키다 means to order food or drinks, or to order someone to do a task. Tasks like 일 (work) or 심부름 (an errand) are its usual objects, and the person given the task takes ~에게.

examples.en: We ordered pizza.
Mom sent me on an errand.
My manager gives me a lot of work.
What shall we order?

grammar.explanation: Attach ~이나 to a noun ending in a consonant or ~나 to one ending in a vowel to offer it as one of the choices, like 'or'. It can join subjects or objects. When both options would take the same particle (~에서, ~(으)로), the particle usually appears only after the second one.

examples.en: I will eat bread or rice.

examples.ko: 엄마나 아빠가 저를 학교에 데려다 줄 거예요.
examples.en: Mom or dad will take me to school.
Shall I get you coffee or tea?
I'll go by bus or taxi.

grammar.point: Settling for something: ~(이)나 with one option
grammar.explanation: When ~(이)나 is attached to only one noun, it can mean the speaker is settling for that option, which is not their first choice. It gives a 'just... I guess' feeling and is often used in suggestions.

examples.en: There's nothing to do, so let's just watch TV.
I'm hungry, so shall we just have ramen?
I'm tired, so I guess I'll just sleep at home.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~거나 to a verb or adjective stem to say 'do A or do B'. The last verb carries the tense and politeness. ~(이)나 chooses between nouns, while ~거나 chooses between actions or states.

examples.en: On weekends I read or exercise.
I'll write my friend a letter or call him.
If you're tired or sick, rest at home.
In the evening I listen to music or take a walk.
